{{short description|Superconformal Yang–Mills theory}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''N'' = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory}}
{{more citations needed|date=September 2012}}
{{String theory|cTopic=Theory}}
'''''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills''' ('''SYM''') '''theory''' is a [[special relativity|relativistic]] [[conformal symmetry|conformally invariant]] [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] [[gauge theory]] describing the interactions of [[fermion]]s via [[gauge field]] exchanges. In ''D''=4 [[spacetime]] dimensions, ''N''=4 is the maximal number of [[supersymmetry|supersymmetries]] or supersymmetry charges.<ref name="SYM TASI01 lectures">{{cite book |doi=10.1142/9789812702821_0001|chapter=Supersymmetric Gauge Theories and the Ads/CFT Correspondence |title=Strings, Branes and Extra Dimensions |year=2004 |last1=d'Hoker |first1=Eric |last2=Freedman |first2=Daniel Z. |pages=3–159 |arxiv=hep-th/0201253 |isbn=978-981-238-788-2 |s2cid=119501374 }}</ref> 

SYM theory is a [[toy theory]] based on [[Yang–Mills theory]]; it does not model the real world, but it is useful because it can act as a proving ground for approaches for attacking problems in more complex theories.<ref>{{cite web|publisher=[[Ars Technica]]|title=Earning a PhD by studying a theory that we know is wrong|author=Matt von Hippel|url=https://arstechnica.com/science/2013/05/earning-a-phd-by-studying-a-theory-that-we-know-is-wrong/|date=2013-05-21}}</ref> It describes a universe containing [[bosonic field|boson field]]s and [[fermion field]]s which are related by four [[Supersymmetry|supersymmetries]] (this means that transforming bosonic and fermionic fields in a certain way leaves the theory invariant). It is one of the simplest (in the sense that it has no free parameters except for the [[gauge group]]) and one of the few [[Ultraviolet divergence|ultraviolet finite]] [[quantum field theory|quantum field theories]] in 4 dimensions. It can be thought of as the most symmetric field theory that does not involve gravity.

Like all supersymmetric field theories, SYM theory may equivalently be formulated as a [[superfield]] theory on an extended [[superspace]] in which the spacetime variables are augmented by a number of [[Grassmann number|Grassmann variables]] which, for the case ''N''=4, consist of 4 [[Dirac spinor]]s, making a total of 16 independent anticommuting generators for the extended [[ring (algebra)|ring]] of superfunctions. The [[field equation]]s are equivalent to the geometric condition that the [[curvature 2-form|supercurvature 2-form]] vanish identically on all super [[null vector|null line]]s.<ref name="W1">{{cite journal | first1=E. | last1=Witten  | title=An interpretation of classical Yang-Mills theory | journal=Phys. Lett.  | volume=77B | pages=394–398 | year=1978 | issue=4–5 | doi= 10.1016/0370-2693(78)90585-3 | bibcode=1978PhLB...77..394W }}</ref><ref name="HHLS">{{cite journal |first1=J. | last1=Harnad | first2=J. | last2=Hurtubise |first3=M. | last3=Légaré | first4=S. | last4=Shnider| title=Constraint equations and field equations in supersymmetric N = 3 Yang-Mills theory | journal=Nuclear Physics  | volume=B256 | pages=609–620 | year=1985 | doi= 10.1016/0550-3213(85)90410-9 | bibcode=1985NuPhB.256..609H }}</ref> This is also known as the [[Twistor theory|super-ambitwistor correspondence]].

A similar super-ambitwistor characterization holds for ''D''=10, ''N''=1 dimensional super Yang–Mills theory,<ref name="W2">{{cite journal | first1=E. | last1=Witten  | title=Twistor-like transform in ten dimensions | journal=Nuclear Physics  |  volume=B266 | pages=245–264 | year=1986 | issue=2 | doi= 10.1016/0550-3213(86)90090-8 | bibcode=1986NuPhB.266..245W }}</ref><ref name="HS">{{cite journal | first1=J. | last1=Harnad | first2=S. | last2=Shnider | title=Constraints and Field Equations for Ten Dimensional Super Yang-Mills Theory | journal=Commun. Math. Phys.  | volume=106 | pages=183–199 | year=1986 | issue=2 | doi= 10.1007/BF01454971 | bibcode=1986CMaPh.106..183H | s2cid=122622189 | url=http://projecteuclid.org/euclid.cmp/1104115696 }}</ref> and the lower dimensional cases ''D''=6, ''N''=2 and ''D''=4, ''N''=4 may be derived from this via [[Yang-Mills_ equations#Dimensional reduction and other moduli spaces|dimensional reduction]].

==Meaning of ''N'' and numbers of fields ==
In ''N'' supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory, ''N'' denotes the number of independent supersymmetric operations that transform the [[Spin (physics)|spin]]-1 gauge field into spin-1/2 fermionic fields.<ref name="4 gravitons blog, N=4">[https://4gravitons.com/n4-maximal-particles-for-maximal-fun/ "''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4: Maximal Particles for Maximal Fun", from ''4 gravitons'' blog (2013)]</ref> In an analogy with symmetries under rotations, ''N'' would be the number of independent rotations, ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1 in a plane, ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2 in 3D space, etc... That is, in a ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 SYM theory, the gauge boson can be "rotated" into ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 different supersymmetric fermion partners. In turns, each fermion can be rotated into four different bosons: one corresponds to the rotation back to the spin-1 gauge field, and the three others are spin-0 boson fields. Because in 3D space one may use different rotations to reach a same point (or here the same spin-0 boson), each spin-0 boson is superpartners of two different spin-1/2 fermions, not just one.<ref name="4 gravitons blog, N=4"/> So in total, one has only 6 spin-0 bosons, not 16.

Therefore, ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 SYM has 1&nbsp;+&nbsp;4&nbsp;+&nbsp;6&nbsp;=&nbsp;11 fields, namely: one vector field (the spin-1 gauge boson), four spinor fields (the spin-1/2 fermions) and six scalar fields (the spin-0 bosons). ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 is the maximum number of independent supersymmetries: starting from a spin-1 field and using more supersymmetries, e.g., ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5, only rotates between the 11 fields. To have ''N''&nbsp;>&nbsp;4 independent supersymmetries, one needs to start from a gauge field of spin higher than 1, e.g., a spin-2 [[tensor]] field such as that of the [[graviton]]. This is the [[N = 8 supergravity|''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;8 supergravity]] theory.

==Lagrangian==
The [[Lagrangian (field theory)|Lagrangian]] for the theory is<ref name="SYM TASI01 lectures"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www-hep.physics.uiowa.edu/~vincent/courses/29276/Presentations/Luke%20Wassink.pdf|title=''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 Super Yang–Mills theory|author=Luke Wassink|year=2009|access-date=2013-05-22|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140531090415/http://www-hep.physics.uiowa.edu/~vincent/courses/29276/Presentations/Luke%20Wassink.pdf|archive-date=2014-05-31}}</ref>
: <math>L = \operatorname{tr} \left\{-\frac{1}{2g^2}F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+\frac{\theta_I}{8\pi^2}F_{\mu\nu}\bar{F}^{\mu\nu}- i \overline{\lambda}^a\overline{\sigma}^\mu D_\mu \lambda_a -D_\mu X^i D^\mu X^i
+g C^{ab}_i \lambda_a[X^i,\lambda_b] + g \overline{C}_{iab}\overline{\lambda}^a[X^i,\overline{\lambda}^b]+\frac{g^2}{2}[X^i,X^j]^2 \right\},
</math>
where <math> g </math> and <math> \theta_I </math> are [[coupling constant]]s (specifically <math> g </math> is the gauge coupling and <math> \theta_I </math> is the [[instanton]] angle), 
the [[Field strength tensor|field strength]] is <math> F^k_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^k_\nu-\partial_\nu A^k_\mu+f^{klm}A^l_\mu A^m_\nu </math> 
with <math> A^k_\nu </math> the gauge field
and indices ''i'',''j'' = 1, ..., 6 as well as ''a'', ''b'' = 1, ..., 4, and <math>f</math> represents the [[structure constants]] of the particular gauge group. The <math> \lambda^a </math> are left [[Weyl fermion]]s, <math> \sigma^\mu </math> are the [[Pauli matrices]], <math> D_\mu </math> is the [[gauge covariant derivative]], <math> X^i </math> are real scalars, and <math>C_i^{ab}</math> represents the structure constants of the [[R-symmetry]] group SU(4), which rotates the four supersymmetries. As a consequence of the [[nonrenormalization theorems]], this supersymmetric field theory is in fact a [[Superconformal algebra|superconformal field theory]].

==Ten-dimensional Lagrangian==

The above Lagrangian can be found by beginning with the simpler ten-dimensional Lagrangian

:<math>
L = \operatorname{tr} \left\{ \frac{1}{g^2} F_{IJ} F^{IJ} - i \bar{\lambda} \Gamma^I D_I \lambda \right\},
</math>

where I and J are now run from 0 through 9 and <math>\Gamma^I</math> are the 32 by 32 gamma matrices <math>( 32=2^{10/2} )</math>, followed by adding the term with <math>\theta_I</math> which is a [[Chern class|topological term]].

The components <math>A_i</math> of the gauge field for ''i''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 to 9 become scalars upon eliminating the extra dimensions. This also gives an interpretation of the SO(6) R-symmetry as rotations in the extra compact dimensions.

By compactification on a ''T''<sup>6</sup>, all the [[supercharges]] are preserved, giving ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 in the 4-dimensional theory.

A [[Type IIB string theory]] interpretation of the theory is the worldvolume theory of a stack of [[D-brane|D3-branes]].

==S-duality==

{{Main| S-duality}} {{Main| Montonen–Olive duality }}

The coupling constants <math>\theta_I</math> and <math>g</math> naturally pair together into a single coupling constant

:<math> \tau := \frac{\theta_I}{2\pi}+\frac{4\pi i}{g^2}.</math>

The theory has symmetries that shift <math>\tau</math> by integers. The [[Montonen–Olive duality|S-duality conjecture]] says there is also a symmetry which sends <math> \tau \mapsto \frac{-1}{n_G\tau}</math> as well as switching the group <math>G</math> to its [[Langlands dual group]].

==AdS/CFT correspondence==

{{Main|AdS/CFT correspondence}}

This theory is also important<ref name="SYM TASI01 lectures"/> in the context of the [[holographic principle]]. There is a [[duality (mathematics)|duality]] between [[Type IIB string theory]] on AdS<sub>5</sub> × '''S'''<sup>5</sup> space (a product of 5-dimensional AdS space with a 5-dimensional [[n-sphere|sphere]]) and ''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 super Yang–Mills on the 4-dimensional boundary of AdS<sub>5</sub>. However, this particular realization of the AdS/CFT correspondence is not a realistic model of gravity, since gravity in our universe is 4-dimensional. Despite this, the AdS/CFT correspondence is the most successful realization of the holographic principle, a speculative idea about [[quantum gravity]] originally proposed by [[Gerard 't Hooft]], who was expanding on work on black hole thermodynamics, and was improved and promoted in the context of string theory by [[Leonard Susskind]].

==Integrability <!--'Planar limit', 'Planar Yang-Mills theory', and 'Planar Yang-Mills theory' redirect here--> ==
There is evidence that ''[[Extended supersymmetry|N]]'' = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory has an integrable structure in the planar [[Large N limit|large ''N'' limit]] (see below for what "planar" means in the present context).<ref>{{cite book |doi=10.1017/CBO9780511846373.008|chapter=Integrability and scattering amplitudes |title=Gauge/Gravity Duality |year=2015 |pages=240–272 |isbn=9780511846373|last1=Ammon |first1=Martin|last2=Erdmenger |first2=Johanna|author2-link=Johanna Erdmenger }}</ref> As the number of colors (also denoted ''N'') goes to infinity, the amplitudes scale like <math>N^{2-2g}</math>, so that only the [[Planar graph|genus 0 (planar graph)]] contribution survives. '''Planar [[Feynman diagrams]]''' are graphs in which no [[propagator]] cross over another one, in contrast to '''non-planar Feynman graphs''' where one or more propagator goes over another one.<ref>[https://4gravitons.com/2013/09/27/planar-vs-non-planar-a-colorful-story/ "Planar vs. Non-Planar: A Colorful Story", from ''4 gravitons'' blog (2013)]</ref> A non-planar graph has a smaller number of possible gauge loops compared to a similar planar graph. Non-planar graphs are thus suppressed by factors <math>1/N^{2-2g}</math> compared to planar ones which therefore dominate in the large ''N'' limit. Consequently, a '''planar Yang–Mills theory'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> denotes a theory in the large ''N'' limit, with ''N'' usually the number of [[color charge|color]]s. Likewise, a '''planar limit'''<!--boldface per WP:R#PLA--> is a limit in which scattering amplitudes are dominated by [[Feynman diagrams]] which can be given the structure of planar graphs.<ref>[https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/planar+limit planar limit in nLab]</ref> In the [[large N limit|large ''N'' limit]], the coupling <math> g </math> vanishes and a [[Perturbation theory (quantum mechanics)|perturbative formalism]] is therefore well-suited for large ''N'' calculations. Therefore, planar graphs are associated to the domain where perturbative calculations converge well.

[[Niklas Beisert|Beisert]] et al. <ref name="Beisert">{{cite journal| first=Niklas |last=Beisert |title=Review of AdS/CFT Integrability: An Overview |journal=Letters in Mathematical Physics |volume=99|date=January 2012|issue=1–3 |page=425|arxiv = 1012.4000 |bibcode = 2012LMaPh..99..425K |doi = 10.1007/s11005-011-0516-7 |s2cid=254796664 }}</ref> give a review article demonstrating how in this situation local operators can be expressed via certain states in [[spin chain]]s (in particular the [[Heisenberg spin chain]]), but based on a larger [[Lie superalgebra]] rather than <math>\mathfrak{su}(2)</math> for ordinary spin. These spin chains are integrable in the sense that they can be solved by the [[Bethe ansatz]] method. They also construct an [[algebra representation|action]] of the associated [[Yangian]] on [[scattering amplitudes]].

[[Nima Arkani-Hamed]] et al. have also researched this subject. Using [[twistor theory]], they find a description (the [[amplituhedron]] formalism) in terms of the positive [[Grassmannian]].<ref name="Arkani-Hamed2012">{{cite arXiv|eprint=1212.5605|first1=Nima |last1=Arkani-Hamed|first2=Jacob L. | last2=Bourjaily|first3=Freddy|last3= Cachazo | first4=Alexander B.|last4=Goncharov|first5=Alexander |last5= Postnikov|first6=Jaroslav |last6= Trnka|title=Scattering Amplitudes and the Positive Grassmannian|year=2012|class=hep-th }}</ref>

==Relation to 11-dimensional M-theory==
''N''&nbsp;=&nbsp;4 super Yang–Mills can be derived from a simpler 10-dimensional theory, and yet [[eleven-dimensional supergravity|supergravity]] and [[M-theory]] exist in 11 dimensions. The connection is that if the gauge group U(''N'') of SYM becomes infinite as <math>N\rightarrow \infty</math> it becomes equivalent to an 11-dimensional theory known as [[matrix theory (physics)|matrix theory]].{{citation needed|date=August 2018}}

== Topologically twisted N = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory ==
N = 4 supersymmetric Yang–Mills theory can be topologically twisted. Such a twist is a choice for how the four-dimensional [[spin group]] <math>\operatorname{Spin}(4)=\operatorname{SU}(2)\times\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> acts on the canonical inclusion [[Representation theory|representation]] <math>\mathbf{4}\colon\operatorname{SU}(4)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{GL}_4(\mathbb{C})</math> of the [[R-symmetry]] group, which relates the [[topology]] to the supersymmetry. Three inequivalent twists exists, which are the [[Donaldson–Witten twist]]<math>(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1})</math>, the [[Vafa–Witten twist]] <math>(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2})</math> and the [[Kapustin–Witten twist]]<math>(\mathbf{2},\mathbf{1})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{2})</math>.<ref name=":0">Manshot 23, p. 11-14</ref>
